verses.text: The brothers the Jews that be at Jerusalem, and in the lande of Iudea, wish to the brothers the Jews that are throughout Egypt, health and peace.
Alahayam be gracious to you, and remember his Couenant that he made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithfull servants:
And give you all an heart to serve him, and to do his will, with a good courage, and a willing mind:
And open your hearts in his law and commandements, & send you peace:
And heare your prayers, and be at one with you, and never forsake you in time of trouble.
And now we be here praying for you.

What time as Demetrius reigned, in the hundred threescore and ninth yeere, we the Jews wrote to you, in the extremitie of trouble, that came on us in those yeeres, from the time that Iason and his company reuolted from the holy land, and kingdome,
And burnt the porch, and shed innocent blood. Then we prayed to the Lord, and were heard: we offered also sacrifices, and fine flowre, and lighted the lampes, and set forth the loaues.
And now see that you keepe the feast of Tabernacles in the moneth Casleu.

In the hundreth, fourescore, and eight yeere, the people that were at Jerusalem, and in Iudea, and the counsel, and Judas, sent greeting and health to Aristobulus, king Ptolomeus master, who was of the stock of the anointed priests, and to the Jews that were in Egypt.
Insomuch as Alahayam has deliuered us from great perils, we thanke him highly, as hauing bin in battell against a king.
For he cast them out that fought within the holy city.
For when the leader was come into Persia, and the armie with him that seemed inuincible, they were slaine in the temple of Nanea, by the deceit of Naneas priests.
For Antiochus, as though he would marrie her, came into the place, and his friends that were with him, to receive money in name of a dowrie.
Which when the priests of Nanea had set forth, and he was entred with a small company into the compasse of the temple, they shut the temple assoone as Antiochus was come in.
And opening a priuie doore of the roofe, they threw stones like thunderbolts, and stroke down the captaine, hewed them in pieces, smote off their heads, and cast them to those that were without.
Blessed be our Alahayam in all things, who has deliuered up the ungodly.

Therefore whereas we are nowe purposed to keep the purification of the Temple on the five & twentieth day of the moneth Casleu, we thought it necessary to certifie you of it, that you also might keepe it, as the of the tabernacles, and of the fire when Neemias offered sacrifice, after that he had builded the Temple, and the Altar.

For when our fathers were led into Persia, the Priests that were then deuout, took the fire of the Altar priuily, & hid it in a hollow place of a pit without water, where they kept it sure, so that the place was unknown to all men.

Now after many yeeres, when it pleased Alahayam, Neemias being sent from the king of Persia, did send of the posteritie of those Priests that had hid it, to the fire: but when they tolde us they found no fire, but thicke water,
Then cōmanded he them to draw it up, and to bring it: and when the sacrifices were laid on, Neemias cōmanded the Priests to sprinkle þ wood, and the things laid thereupon with þ water.
When this was done, and the time came that the Sun shone which afore was hid in the cloude, there was a great fire kindled, so that every man marueiled.
And the Priests made a prayer whilest the sacrifice was consuming, both the Priests, and all the rest, Ionathan beginning, and the rest answering thereunto, as Neemias did.
And the prayer was after this maner, O Lord, Lord Alahayam, Creatour of all things, who are fearefull, and strong, and righteous, and mercifull, and the only, and gracious king,
The only giuer of all things, the only just, almightie & euerlasting, you that deliuerest Yahsharala from al trouble, & did choose the fathers, & sanctifie them:
Receive the sacrifice for your whole people Yahsharala, and preserue your own portion, and sanctifie it.
Gather those together that are scattered frō us, deliuer them that serve among the heathen, looke on them that are despised & abhorred, and let the heathen know that you are our Alahayam.
Punish them that oppresse us, and with pride do us wrong.
Plant your people again in your holy place, as Moises has spoken.
And the Priests sung psalmes of thankesgiuing.
Now when the sacrifice was consumed, Neemias commanded the water that was left, to be powred on the great stones.
When this was done, there was kindled a flame: but it was consumed by the light that shined from the Altar.

So when this matter was knowen, it was told the king of Persia, that in the place, where the Priests that were led away, had hid the fire, there appeared water, and that Neemias had purified the sacrifices with it.
Then the king inclosing the place, made it holy after he had tried þ matter.
And the king tooke many gifts, and bestowed of it, on those whom he would gratifie.
And Neemias called this thing Naphthar, which is as much to say as a cleansing: but many men call it Nephi.
It is also found in the records, that Ieremie the Prophet, commaunded them that were caried away, to take of the fire as it has been signified,

And how that the Prophet hauing given them the law, charged them not to forget the commaundements of the Lord, and that they should not erre in their minds, when they see images of siluer, and gold, with their ornaments.
And with other such speeches exhorted he them, that the law should not depart from their hearts.

It was also contained in the same writing, that the Prophet being warned of Alahayam, commanded the Tabernacle, and the Arke to goe with him, as he went forth into the mountaine, where Moises climed up, and sawe the heritage of Alahayam.
And when Ieremie came thither, he found an hollow caue wherin he laid the Tabernacle, and the Arke, and the altar of incense, & so stopped the doore.
And some of those that followed him, came to marke the way, but they could not find it.
Which when Ieremie perceiued, he blamed them, saying, As for that place, it shall be unknown until the time that Alahayam gather his people again together, and receive them to mercy.

Then shall the Lord show them these things, and the glory of the Lord shall appeare, and the cloud also as it was showed under Moises, and as when Solomon desired that the place might be honourably sanctified.
It was also declared that he being wise, offered the sacrifice of dedication, and of the finishing of the Temple.
And as when Moises prayed to the Lord, the fire came down from heaven, and consumed the sacrifices: even so prayed Solomon also, and the fire came down from heaven, and consumed the burnt offerings.
And Moises said, because the sin offering was not to be eaten, it was consumed.
So Solomon kept those eight days.

The same things also were reported in the writings, and commentaries of Neemias, and how he founding a librarie, gathered together the acts of the Kings, and the Prophets, and of Dauid, and the Epistles of the Kings concerning the holy gifts.
In like maner also, Judas gathered together all those things that were lost, by reason of the warre we had, and they remaine with us.
Therefore if you have neede of it, send some to fetch them to you.
Whereas we then are about to celebrate the purification, we have written to you, and you shall do well if you keepe the same days.
We hope also that the Alahayam, that deliuered all his people, and gave them all an heritage, and the kingdome, and the priesthood, and the Sanctuarie,

As he promised in the lawe, will shortly have mercy on us, and gather us together out of every land under heaven into the holy place: for he has deliuered us out of great troubles, and has purified the place.
Now as concerning Judas Maccabeus, and his brothers, and the purification of the great Temple, and the dedication of the altar,
And the warres against Antiochus Epiphanes, & Eupator his son,

And the manifest signes that came from heaven, to those that behaued themselues manfully to their honour for Iudaisme: so that being but a few, they ouercame the whole country, and chased barbarous multitudes,
And recouered again the Temple renowned all the world over, and freed the city, and vpheld the lawes, which were going down, the Lord being gracious to them with al favor:
All these things (I say) being declared by Iason of Cyrene in five books, we will assay to abridge in one volume.
For considering the infinite number, and the difficulty, which they find that desire to looke into the narrations of the story, for the variety of þ matter,
We have been carefull, that they that will read might have delight, and that they that are desirous to commit to memorie, might have ease, and that all, into whose hands it comes might have profit.
Therefore to us that have taken on us this paineful labour of abridging, it was not easie, but a matter of sweat, and watching.
Even as it is no ease to him, that prepareth a banquet, and seeks the benefit of others: yet for the pleasuring of many we will vndertake gladly this great paines:
Leauing to the authour the exact handling of every particular, and labouring to follow the rules of an abridgement.

For as the master builder of a new house, must care for the whole building: but he that vndertaketh to set it out, and paint it, must seeke out fit things for the adorning of it: even so I thinke it is with us.
To stand on every point, and goe over things at large, and to be curious in particulars, belongeth to the first authour of the storie.
But to use breuitie, and auoyde much labouring of the worke, is to be granted to him that will make an abridgement.
Here then will we begin the story: only adding thus much to that which has been said, That it is a foolish thing to make a long prologue, and to be short in the story it self.
Now when the holy City was inhabited with all peace, and the Lawes were kept very well, because of the godlinesse of Onias the high Priest, and his hatred of wickednesse,
It came to passe that even the Kings themselues did honour the place, and magnifie the Temple with their best gifts;
Insomuch that Seleucus king of Asia, of his own reuenues, bare all the costes belonging to the seruice of the sacrifices.
But one Simon of the tribe of Beniamin, who was made gouernour of the Temple, fell out with the high Priest about disorder in the city.
And when he could not overcome Onias, he gate him to Apollonius the son of Thraseas, who then was gouernour of Coelosyria, and Phenice,

And told him that the treasurie in Jerusalem was full of infinite summes of money, so that the multitude of their riches which did not pertaine to the account of the sacrifices, was innumerable, and that it was possible to bring all into the kings hand.

Now when Apollonius came to the king, and had showed him of the money, whereof he was told, the king chose out Heliodorus his treasurer, and sent him with a commaundement, to bring him the foresaid money.
So foorthwith Heliodorus tooke his iourney under a colour of visiting the cities of Coelosyria, and Phenice, but indeed to fulfill the kings purpose.

And when he was come to Jerusalem, & had been courteously received of the high Priest of the city, he told him what intelligence was given of the money, & declared therefore he came, and and asked if these things were so in deed.
Then the high Priest tolde him that there was such money layde up for the reliefe of widowes, and fatherlesse children,

And that some of it belonged to Hircanus, son of Tobias, a man of great dignitie, and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed: the summe whereof in all was four hundred talents of siluer, and two hundred of gold,

And that it was altogether impossible that such wrong should be done to them, that had committed it to the holiness of the place, and to the maiestie and inuiolable sanctitie of the Temple, honoured over all the world.
But Heliodorus because of the kings commandement given him, said, That in any wise it must be brought into the kings treasury.
So at the day which he appointed, he entred in to order this matter, therefore, there was no small agonie throughout the whole city.

But the Priests prostrating themselues before the Altar in their Priests Uestments, called to heaven on him that made a Lawe concerning things given to be kept, that they should safely be preserued for such as had committed them to be kept.
Then whoever had looked the hie Priest in the face, it would have wounded his heart: for his countenance, and the changing of his colour, declared the inward agonie of his mind:
For the man was so compassed with fear, and horror of the body, that it was manifest to them that looked on him, what sorrow he had now in his heart.
Others ran flocking out of their houses to the generall Supplication, because the place was like to come into contempt.

And the women girt with sackecloth under their breasts, abounded in the streetes, and the virgins that were kept in, ran some to the gates, and some to the walles, and others looked out of the windowes:
And all holding their handes towards heaven, made supplication.
Then it would have pitied a man to see the falling down of the multitude of all sorts, and the fear of the hie Priest, being in such an agony.
They then called on the Almightie Lord, to keepe the things committed of trust, safe and sure, for those that had committed them.
Neuerthelesse Heliodorus executed that which was decreed.

Now as he was there present himself with his guard about the treasurie, the Lord of spirits, & the Prince of all power caused a great apparition, so that all that presumed to come in with him, were astonished at the power of Alahayam, and fainted, and were sore afraid.

For there appeared to them a horse, with a terrible rider on him, and adorned with a very faire couering, and he ranne fiercely, and smote at Heliodorus with his forefeet, and it seemed that he that sate on the horse, had complete harnesse of golde.

Moreouer two other yong men appeared before him, notable in strength, excellent in beautie, and comely in apparell, who stood by him on either side, and scourged him continually, and gave him many sore stripes.
And Heliodorus fell suddenly to the ground, and was compassed with great darkness: but they that were with him, tooke him up, and put him into a litter.

Thus him that lately came with a great traine, and with all his guard into the said treasury, they caried out, being vnable to helpe himself with his weapons: and manifestly they acknowledged the power of Alahayam.
For he by the hand of Alahayam was cast down, and lay speechlesse without all hope of life.

But they praised the Lord that had miraculously honoured his own place: for the Temple which a little afore was full of fear and trouble, when the Almightie Lord appeared, was filled with ioy and gladnesse.
Then straightwayes certain of Heliodorus friends, prayed Onias that he would call on the most High to graunt him his life, who lay ready to give up the ghost.
So the high Priest suspecting lest the king should misconceiue that some treachery had been done to Heliodorus by the Jews, offered a sacrifice for the health of the man.

Now as the high Priest was making an atonement, the same yong men, in the same clothing, appeared and stood beside Heliodorus, saying, Give Onias the high Priest great thankes, insomuch as for his sake the Lord has granted you life.
And seeing that you have been scourged from heaven, declare to all men the mightie power of Alahayam: and when they had spoken these wordes, they appeared no more.
So Heliodorus after he had offered sacrifice to the Lord, and made great vowes to him that had saved his life, and saluted Onias, returned with his hoste to the king.
Then testified he to all men, the workes of the great Alahayam, which he had seene with his eyes.
And when the king asked Heliodorus, who might be a fit man to be sent yet once again to Jerusalem, he said,
If you have any enemy or traitor, send him thither, and you will receive him well scourged, if he escape with his life: for in that place, no doubt, there is an especiall power of Alahayam.
For he that dwells in heaven has his eye on that place, and defendeth it, and he beateth and destroyeth them that come to hurt it.
And the things concerning Heliodorus, and the keeping of the treasurie, fell out on this sort.
This Simon now (of whō we spake afore) hauing bin a bewrayer of the money, and of his country, slandered Onias, as if he had terrified Heliodorus, and been the worker of these euils.
Thus was he bold to call him a traitour, that had deserued well of the city, and tendred his own nation, and was so zealous of the lawes.
But when their hatred went so farre, that by one of Simons faction murthers were committed,
Onias seeing the danger of this contention, and that Appollonius, as being the gouernour of Coelosyria and Phenice, did rage, and increase Simons malice,
He went to the king, not to be an accuser of his country men, but seeking the good of all, both publike, & priuate.
For he saw that it was impossible, that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leaue his folly, vnlesse the king did looke thereunto.
But after the death of Seleucus, when Antiochus called Epiphanes, tooke the kingdom, Iason the brother of Onias, laboured under hand to be hie Priest,
Promising to the king by intercession, three hundred and threescore talents of siluer, and of another reuenew, eighty talents:

Besides this, he promised to assigne an hundred and fifty more, if he might have licence to set him up a place for exercise, and for the training up of youth in the fashions of the heathen, and to write them of Jerusalem Antiochians.
Which when the king had granted, and he had gotten into his hand the rule, he foorthwith brought his own nation to the Greekish fashion.

And the royal priuiledges granted of speciall favor to the Jews, by the meanes of Iohn the father of Eupolemus, who went Embassador to Rome, for amitie and aid, he tooke away, and putting down the gouernments which were according to the law, he brought up new customes against the law.
For he built gladly a place of exercise under the towre it self, and brought the chiefe yong men under his subiection, and made them weare a hat.
Now such was the height of Greek fashions, and increase of heathenish maners, through the exceeding profanenes of Iason that ungodly wretch, and no high priest:

That the priests had no courage to serve any more at the altar, but despising the Temple, and neglecting the sacrifices, hastened to be partakers of the vnlawfull allowance in the place of exercise, after the game of Discus called them forth.
Not setting by the honours of their fathers, but liking the glory of the Grecians best of all.
By reason whereof sore calamity came on them: for they had them to be their enemies and auengers, whose custome they followed so earnestly, and to whom they desired to be like in all things.
For it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the lawes of Alahayam, but the time following shall declare these things.
Now when the game that was used every fift yere was kept at Tyrus, the king being present,

This vngracious Iason sent speciall messengers from Jerusalem, who were Antiochians, to carie three hundred drachmes of siluer to the sacrifice of Hercules, which even the bearers therof thought fit not to bestow on the sacrifice, because it was not conuenient, but to be reserued for other charges.
This money then in regard of the sender, was appointed to Hercules sacrifice, but because of the bearers of it, it was imployed to the making of gallies.

Now when Apollonius the son of Manastheus was sent to Egypt, for the coronation of king Ptolomeus Philometor, Antiochus understanding him not to be well affected to his affaires, provided for his own safetie: whereupon he came to Ioppe, & from thence to Jerusalem.
Where he was honourably received of Iason, and of the city, and was brought in with torchlight, and with great shoutings: and so afterward went with his hoste to Phenice.
Three yeere afterward, Iason sent Menelaus the foresaid Simons brother, to beare the money to the king, and to put him in mind of certain necessary matters.

But he being brought to the presence of the king, when he had magnified him, for the glorious appearance of his power, got the priesthood to himself, offering more then Iason by three hundred talents of siluer.
So he came with the kings Mandate, bringing nothing worthy the high priesthood, but hauing the fury of a cruell Tyrant, and the rage of a sauage beast.
Then Iason, who had vndermined his own brother, being vndermined by another, was cōpelled to flee into the country of the Ammonites.
So Menelaus got the principalitie: but as for the money that he had promised to the king, he tooke no good order for it, albeit Sostratus the ruler of the castle required it.
For to him appertained the gathering of the customes. Therefore they were both called before the king.
Now Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus in his stead in the priesthood, and Sostratus left Crates, who was gouernour of the Cyprians.
While those things were in doing, they of Tharsus and Mallos made insurrection, because they were given to the kings concubine called Antiochis.
Then came the king in all haste to appease matters, leauing Andronicus a man in authority, for his deputy.

Now Menelaus supposing that he had gotten a conuenient time, stole certain vessels of gold, out of the temple, and gave some of them to Andronicus, and some he sold into Tyrus, and the cities round about.
Which when Onias knew of a surety, he reprooued him, and withdrew himself into a Sanctuarie at Daphne, that lieth by Antiochia.

Therefore Menelaus, taking Andronicus apart, prayed him to get Onias into his hands, who being perswaded thereunto, and comming to Onias in deceit, gave him his right hand with othes, and though he were suspected (by him) yet perswaded he him to come forth of the Sanctuarie: whom forthwith he shut up without regard of Justice.
For the which cause not only the Jews, but many also of other nations tooke great indignation, and were much grieued for the vniust murder of the man.

And when the king was come again from the places about Cilicia, the Jews that were in the city, and certain of the Greekes, that abhorred the fact also, complained because Onias was slaine without cause.
Therefore Antiochus was heartily sorry, and mooued to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behauiour of him that was dead.

And being kindled with anger, forthwith he tooke away Andronicus his purple, and rent off his clothes, and leading him through the whole city to that very place, where he had committed impietie against Onias, there slew he the cursed murtherer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserued.

Now when many sacriledges had been committed in the city by Lysimachus, with the consent of Menelaus, and the bruit therof was spread abroad, the multitude gathered themselues together against Lysimachus, many vessels of gold being already caried away.

Whereupon the common people rising, and being filled with rage, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men, and beganne first to offer violence on Auranus, being the leader, a man farre gone in yeeres, & no lesse in folly.

They then seeing the attempt of Lysimachus, some of them caught stones, some clubs, others taking handfuls of dust, that was next at hand, cast them all together on Lysimachus, and those that set on them.
Thus many of them they wounded, & some they stroke to the ground, and all they forced to flee: but as for the Churchrobber himself, him they killed besides the treasury.
Of these matters therefore there was an accusation laide against Menelaus.
Now when the king came to Tyrus, three men that were sent from the Senate, pleaded the cause before him:
But Menelaus being now conuicted, promised Ptolomee the son of Dorymenes, to give him much money, if he would pacifie the King towards him.
Whereupon Ptolomee taking the king aside into a certain gallerie, as it were to take the aire, brought him to be of another mind;

Insomuch that he discharged Menelaus from the accusations, who notwithstanding was cause of all the mischiefe: and those poore men, who if they had told their cause, yea, before the Scythians, should have been iudged innocent, them he condemned to death.
Thus they that followed the matter for the city, and for the people, and for the holy vessels, did soone suffer vniust punishment.
Therefore even they of Tyrus mooued with hatred of that wicked deed, caused them to be honourably buried.
And so through the couetousnesse of them that were in power, Menelaus remained still in authority, increasing in malice, and being a great traitour to the citizens.
About the same time Antiochus prepared his second voyage into Egypt:

And then it happened, that through all the city, for the space almost of fourtie days, there were seene horsemen running in the aire, in cloth of golde, and armed with lances, like a band of souldiers,

And troupes of horsemen in aray, incountring, and running one against another with shaking of shieldes, and multitude of pikes, and drawing of swords, and casting of darts, and glittering of golden ornaments, and harnesse of all sorts.
Therefore every man praied that that apparition might turne to good.

Now when there was gone forth a false rumour, as though Antiochus had been dead, Iason tooke at the least a thousand men, and suddenly made an assault on the city, and they that were on the walles, being put backe, and the city at length taken, Menelaus fled into the castle:

But Iason slew his own citizens without mercy, (not considering that to get the day of them of his own nation, would be a most unhappy day for him: but thinking they had been his enemies, and not his country men whom he conquered.)
Howbeit, for all this he obtained not the principalitie, but at the last received shame for the reward of his treason, and fled again into the country of the Ammonites.

In the end therefore he had an unhappy returne, being accused before Aretas the king of the Arabians, fleeing from city to city, pursued of all men, hated as a forsaker of the Lawes, and being had in abomination, as an open enemie of his country, and countreymen, he was cast out into Egypt.
Thus he that had driuen many out of their country, perished in a strange land, retiring to the Lacedemonians, and thinking there to finde succour by reason of his kindred.
And he that had cast out many vnburied, had none to mourne for him, nor any solemne funerals at all, nor sepulchre with his fathers.
Now when this that was done came to the kings eare, he thought that Iudea had reuolted, whereupon remouing out of Egypt in a furious mind, he tooke the city by force of armes,
And commaunded his men of warre not to spare such as they met, and to slay such as went up on the houses.
Thus there was killing of yong and old, making away of men, women and children, slaying of virgins and infants.
And there were destroyed within the space of three whole daies, fourescore thousand, whereof fourty thousand were slaine in the conflict; and no fewer sold, then slaine.
Yet was he not content with this, but presumed to goe into the most holy Temple of all the world: Menelaus that traitour to the Lawes, and to his own country, being his guide.

And taking the holy vessels with polluted handes, and with prophane handes, pulling down the things that were dedicated by other kings, to the augmentation and glory and honour of the place, he gave them away.
And so haughtie was Antiochus in mind, that he considered not that the Lord was angry for a while for the sins of them that dwelt in the city, and therefore his eye was not on the place.

For had they not been formerly wrapped in many sins, this man as soone as he had come, had foorthwith been scourged, and put backe from his presumption, as Heliodorus was, whom Seleucus the king sent to view the treasurie.
Neuerthelesse Alahayam did not choose the people for the places sake, but the place for the peoples sake.

And therefore the place it self that was partaker with them of the aduersities that happened to the nation, did afterward communicate in the benefits sent from the Lord: and as it was forsaken in the wrath of the Almighty, so again the great Lord being reconciled, it was set up with all glory.

So when Antiochus had caried out of the Temple, a thousand and eight hundred talents, he departed in all haste into Antiochia, weening in his pride to make the land nauigable, and the Sea passable by foot: such was the haughtinesse of his mind.
And he left gouernours to vexe the nation: at Jerusalem Philip, for his country a Phrygian, and for manners more barbarous then he that set him there:
And at Garizim, Andronicus; and besides, Menelaus, who worse then all the rest, bare an heauie hand over the citizens, hauing a malicious mind against his countreymen the Jews.
He sent also that detestable ringleader Apollonius, with an armie of two and twenty thousand, commaunding him to slay all those that were in their best age, and to sell the women and the yonger sort:
Who comming to Jerusalem, and pretending peace, did forbeare till the holy day of the Sabbath, when taking the Jews keeping holy day, he commanded his men to arme themselues.
And so he slewe all them that were gone to the celebrating of the Sabbath, and running through the city with weapons, slewe great multitudes.

But Judas Maccabeus, with nine others, or thereabout, withdrew himself into the wildernesse, and lived in the mountaines after the maner of beasts, with his company, who fed on herbes continually, lest they should be partakers of the pollution.
Not long after this, the king sent an old man of Athens, to compell the Jews to depart from the lawes of their fathers, and not to live after the Lawes of Alahayam:
And to pollute also the Temple in Jerusalem, and to call it the Temple of Iupiter Olympius: and that in Garizim, of Iupiter the defender of strangers, as they did desire that dwelt in the place.
The comming in of this mischiefe was sore and grieuous to the people:

For the Temple was filled with riot and reuelling, by the Gentiles, who dallied with harlots, and had to do with women within the circuit of the holy places, and besides that, brought in things that were not lawfull.
The Altar also was filled with profane things, which the Law forbiddeth.
Neither was it lawfull for a man to keepe Sabbath days, or ancient Feasts, or to professe himself at all to be a Iewe.

And in the day of the kings birth, every moneth they were brought by bitter constraint to eate of the sacrifices; and when the Feast of Bacchus was kept, the Jews were compelled to goe in procession to Bacchus, carying Iuie.

Moreouer there went out a decree to the neighbour cities of the heathen, by the suggestion of Ptolomee, against the Jews, that they should obserue the same fashions, and be partakers of their sacrifices.
And whoever would not conforme themselues to the maners of the Gentiles, should be put to death: then might a man hane seene the present misery.

For there were two women brought, who had circumcised their children, whom when they had openly led round about the city, the babes hanging at their breasts, they cast them down headlong from the wall.

And others that had run together into caues neere by, to keepe the Sabbath day secretly, being discouered to Philip, were all burnt together, because they made a conscience to helpe themselues, for the honour of the most sacred day.
Now I beseech those that reade this book, that they be not discouraged for these calamities, but that they judge those punishments not to be for destruction, but for a chastening of our nation.
For it is a token of his great goodness, when wicked doers are not suffered any longtime, but forthwith punished.
For not as with other nations whom the Lord patiently forbeareth to punish, till they be come to the fulnesse of their sins, so dealeth he with us,
Lest that being come to the height of sin, afterwards he should take vengeance of us.
And therfore he never withdraweth his mercie from us: and though he punish with aduersitie, yet does he never forsake his people.
But let this that we have spoken be for a warning to us: And nowe will we come to the declaring of the matter in few words.
Eleazar one of the principall Scribes, an aged man, and of a well fauoured countenance, was constrained to open his mouth, and to eate swines flesh.
But he chusing rather to die gloriously, then to live stained with such an abomination, spit it forth, and came of his own accord to the torment,
As it behoued them to come, that are resolute to stand out against such things, as are not lawfull for love of life to be tasted.

But they that had the charge of that wicked feast, for the old acquaintance they had with the man, taking him aside, besought him to bring flesh of his own prouision, such as was lawfull for him to use, and make as if he did eate of the flesh, taken from the sacrifice commanded by the king,
That in so doing he might be deliuered from death, and for the old friendship with them, find favor.

But he began to consider discreetly, and as became his age, and the excellencie of his ancient yeeres, and the honour of his gray head, whereunto he was come, and his most honest education from a child, or rather the holy lawe made, and given by Alahayam: therefore he answered accordingly, and willed them straightwaies to send him to the graue.
For it becommeth not our age, said he, in any wise to dissemble, whereby many yong persons might thinke, that Eleazar being fourescore yeres old and ten, were now gone to a strange religion.
And so they through mine hypocrisie, and desire to live a litle time, and a moment longer, should be deceiued by me, and I get a staine to mine old age, and make it abominable.
For though for the present time I should be deliuered from the punishment of men: yet should I not escape the hand of the Almightie, neither aliue nor dead.
Therefore now manfully changing this life, I will show my self such an one, as mine age requireth,
And leaue a notable example to such as be yong, to die willingly, and couragiously, for the honourable and holy lawes: and when he had said these words, immediatly he went to the torment,
They that led him, changing the good will they bare him a litle before, into hatred, because the foresaid speaches proceeded as they thought, from a desperate mind.

But when he was readie to die with stripes, he groned, and said, It is manifest to the Lord, that has the holy knowledge, that wheras I might have bin deliuered from death, I endure sore paines in body, by being beaten: but in soule am well content to suffer these things, because I fear him.
And thus this man died, leauing his death for an example of a noble courage, and a memoriall of vertue not only to yong men, but to all his nation.
It came to passe also that seven brothers with their mother were taken, and compelled by the king against the lawe to taste swines flesh, and were tormented with scourges, and whips:
But one of them that spake first said thus: What would you aske, or learne of us? we are ready to die, rather then to transgresse the lawes of our fathers.
Then the king being in a rage, commanded pannes, and caldrons to be made whot.
Which forthwith being heated, he commanded to cut out the tongue of him that spake first, and to cut off the vtmost parts of his body, the rest of his brothers, and his mother looking on.

Now when he was thus maimed in all his members, he commanded him being yet aliue, to be brought to the fire, and to be fried in the panne: and as the vapour of the panne was for a good space dispersed, they exhorted one another, with the mother, to die manfully, saying thus:
The Lord Alahayam looketh on us, and in truth has comfort in us, as Moises in his song, which witnessed to their faces declared, saying, And he shall be comforted in his servants.

So when the first was dead, after this maner, they brought the second to make him a mocking stocke: and when they had pulled off the skin of his head with the haire, they asked him, Will you eate before you be punished throughout every member of your body?
But he answered in his own language, and said, No. Therefore he also received the next torment in order, as the former did.
And when he was at the last gaspe, he said, You like a fury takest us out of this present life, but the king of the world shall raise us up, who have died for his lawes, to euerlasting life.
After him was the third made a mocking stocke, and when he was required, he put out his tongue, and that right soone, holding forth his hands manfully,
And said couragiously, These I had from heaven, and for his lawes I despise them, and from him I hope to receive them again.
Insomuch that the king, and they that were with him marueiled at the yong mans courage, for that he nothing regarded the paines.
Now when this man was dead also, they tormented and mangled the fourth in like maner.
So when he was ready to die, he said thus, It is good, being put to death by men, to looke for hope from Alahayam to be raised up again by him: as for you you will have no resurrection to life.
Afterward they brought the fift also, and mangled him.
Then looked he to the king and said, You have power over men, you are corruptible, you doest what you will, yet thinke not that our nation is forsaken of Alahayam.
But abide a while, and behold his great power, how he will torment you, and your seed.

After him also they brought the sixt, who being ready to die, said, Be not deceiued without cause: for we suffer these things for our selues, hauing sinned against our Alahayam. Therefore marueilous things are done (to us.)
But thinke not you that takest in hand to striue against Alahayam, that you will escape vnpunished.

But the mother was marueilous above all, and worthy of honorable memorie: for when she sawe her seven sons slaine within the space of one day, she bare it with a good courage, because of the hope that she had in þ Lord
Yea she exhorted every one of them in her own language, filled with couragious spirits, and stirring up her womanish thoughts, with a manly stomacke, she said to them,
I cannot tell how you came into my wombe: for I neither gave you breath, nor life, neither was it I that formed the mēbers of every one of you.

But doubtlesse the Creator of the world, who formed the generation of man, and found out the beginning of all things, wil also of his own mercy give you breath, and life again, as you now regard not your own selues for his Lawes sake.

Now Antiochus thinking himself despised, and suspecting it to be a reprochfull speach, whiles the yongest was yet aliue, did not only exhort him by wordes, but also assured him with oathes, that he would make him both a rich, and a happy man, if he would turne from the Lawes of his fathers, and that also he would take him for his friend, and trust him with affaires.
But when the yong man would in no case hearken to him, the king called his mother, and exhorted her, that she would counsell the yong man to saue his life.
And when he had exhorted her with many words, she promised him that she would counsell her son.

But she bowing her self towards him, laughing the cruell tyrant to scorne, spake in her country language on this maner; O my son, have pitie on mee that bare you nine moneths in my wombe, and gave you sucke three yeeres, and nourished you, and brought you up to this age, and endured the troubles of education.
I beseech you, my son, looke on the heaven, and the earth, and all that is in it, and consider that Alahayam made them of things that were not, and so was mankinde made likewise;
Fear not this tormentour, but being worthy of your brothers, take your death, that I may receive you again in mercy with your brothers.

Whiles she was yet speaking these words, the yong man said, Whom wait you for? I will not obey the kings commandement: but I will obey the commandement of the Law that was given to our fathers, by Moses.
And you that have been the authour of all mischiefe against the Hebrewes, will not escape the handes of Alahayam.
For we suffer because of our sins.
And though the living Lord be angrie with us a little while for our chastening and correction, yet shall he be at one again, with his servants.
But you, O godlesse man, and of all other most wicked, be not lifted up without a cause, nor puffed up with vncertaine hopes, lifting up your hand against the servants of Alahayam:
For you have not yet escaped the judgment of Almightie Alahayam, who seeth all things.
For our brothers who now have suffered a short paine, are dead under Gods Couenant of euerlasting life: but you through the judgment of Alahayam, will receive just punishment for your pride.

But I, as my brothers, offer up my body, and life for the Lawes of our fathers, beseeching Alahayam that he would speedily be mercifull to our nation, and that you by torments & plagues mayest confesse, that he alone is Alahayam;
And that in me, and my brothers, the wrath of the Almighty, which is iustly brought on all our nation, may cease.
Then the King being in a rage, handled him worse then all the rest, and took it grieuously that he was mocked.
So this man died vndefiled, and put his whole trust in the Lord.
Last of all after the sons, the mother died.
Let this be ynough now to have spoken cōcerning the idolatrous feasts, and the extreme tortures.

Then Judas Maccabeus and they that were with him, went priuily into the townes, and called their kinsefolkes together, and tooke to them all such as continued in the Jews religion, and assembled about six thousand men.
And they called on the Lord, that he would looke on the people that was troden down of all, and also pitie the Temple, prophaned of ungodly men,
And that he would have compassion on the city sore defaced and ready to be made even with the ground, and heare the blood that cried to him,
And remember the wicked slaughter of harmelesse infants, and the blasphemies committed against his Name, and that he would show his hatred against the wicked.
Now when Maccabeus had his company about him, he could not be withstood by the heathen: for the wrath of the Lord was turned into mercy.
Therefore he came at vnawares, and burnt up townes and cities, and got into his hands the most commodious places, and ouercame & put to flight no small number of his enemies.
But specially tooke he aduantage of the night, for such priuie attempts, insomuch that the bruite of his manlinesse was spread every where.

So when Philip sawe that this man encreased by little and little, & that things prospered with him still more and more, he wrote to Ptolemeus, the gouernour of Coelosyria & Phenice, to yeeld more aide to the kings affaires.

Then forthwith choosing Nicanor the son of Patroclus, one of his speciall friends, he sent him with no fewer then twenty thousand of all nations under him, to root out the whole generation of the Jews; and with him he ioyned also Gorgias a captaine, who in matters of warre had great experience.
So Nicanor vndertooke to make so much money of the captiue Jews, as should defray the tribute of two thousand talents, which the king was to pay to the Romanes.

Therefore immediatly he sent to the cities on the sea coast, proclaiming a sale of the captiue Jews, and promising that they should have fourescore and ten bodies for one talent, not expecting the vengeance that was to follow on him from the Almighty Alahayam.
Now when word was brought to Judas of Nicanors cōming, and he had imparted to those that were with him, that the army was at hand,
They that were fearefull, and distrusted the justice of Alahayam, fled, and conueyed themselues away.
Others sold all that they had left, and withall besought the Lord to deliuer them, being solde by the wicked Nicanor before they met together:
And if not for their own sakes, yet for þ couenants he had made with their fathers, and for his holy and glorious Names sake, by which they were called

So Maccabeus called his men together to the number of six thousand, and exhorted them not to be stricken with terrour of the enemie, nor to fear the great multitude of the heathen who came wrongfully against them, but to fight manfully,

And to set before their eyes, the iniury that they had vniustly done to the holy place, and the cruell handling of the city, whereof they made a mockery, and also the taking away of the gouernment of their forefathers:
For they, said he, trust in their weapons and boldnesse, but our confidence is in the Almightie Alahayam, who at a becke can cast down both them that come against us, and also all the world.
Moreouer, he recounted to them what helps their forefathers had found, and how they were deliuered, when under Sennacherib an hundred fourescore and five thousand perished.

And he told them of þ battel that they had in Babylon with the Galatians, how they came but eight thousand in all to þ busines, with four thousand Macedonians, and that the Macedonians being perplexed, the eight thousand destroyed an hundred and twenty thousand, because of the helpe that they had from heaven, & so received a great booty.
Thus when he had made them bold with these words, and ready to die for the Lawes, and the country, he diuided his army into four parts:
And ioyned with himself his own brothers, leaders of each band, to wit, Simon, and Joseph, & Ionathan, giving each one fifteene hundred men.
Also (he appointed) Eleazar to reade the holy book: and when he had given them this watchword, The help of Alahayam; himself leading the first band, he ioyned battell with Nicanor:
And by the helpe of the Almightie, they slew above nine thousand of their enemies, and wounded and maimed the most part of Nicanors hoste, and so put all to flight:
And tooke their money that came to buy them, and pursued them farre: but lacking time, they returned.
For it was the day before the Sabbath, and therefore they would no longer pursue them.

So when they had gathered their armour together, and spoiled their enemies, they occupied themselues about the Sabbath, yeelding exceeding praise, & thanks to the Lord, who had preserued them to þ day, which was the beginning of mercy, distilling on them.
And after the Sabbath, when they had given part of the spoiles to the maimed, and the widdowes, and Orphanes, the residue they diuided among themselues, and their servants.
When this was done, and they had made a common supplication, they besought the mercifull Lord to be reconciled with his servants for ever.

Moreouer of those that were with Timotheus & Bacchides, who fought against them, they slewe above twenty thousand, and very easily got high and strong holds, & diuided among them selues many spoiles more, and made the maimed, orphanes, widowes, yea, & the aged also, equal in spoiles themselues
And when they had gathered their armour together, they laid them up all carefully in couenient places, and the remnant of the spoiles they brought to Jerusalem.
They slew also Philarches that wicked persō who was Timotheus, & had annoied the Jews many waies.

Furthermore at such time as they kept the feast for the victorie in their coūtry, they burnt Calisthenes that had set fire on the holy gates, who was fled into a litle house, and so he received a reward meet for his wickednesse.
As for that most vngracious Nicanor, who had brought a thousand merchants to buy the Jews,

He was through the helpe of the Lord brought down by them, of whō he made least account, & putting off his glorious apparell, and discharging his company, he came like a fugitiue servant through the mid land to Antioch, hauing very great dishonour for that his hoste was destroyed.

Thus he that tooke on him to make good to the Romanes, their tribute by meanes of the captiues in Jerusalem, told abroad, that the Jews had Alahayam to fight for them, and therfore they could not be hurt, because they followed the lawes that he gave them.
About that time came Antiochus with dishonor out of the country of Persia.

For he had entred the city called Persepolis, and went about to rob the Temple, and to hold the city, whereupon the multitude running to defend thēselues with their weapons, put them to flight, & so it happened þ Antiochus being put to flight of the inhabitants, returned with shame.
Now when he came to Ecbatana, newes was brought him what had happened to Nicanor & Timotheus.

Then swelling with anger, he thought to auenge on the Jews the disgrace done to him by those that made him flie. Therfore commanded he his chariot man to driue without ceasing, and to dispatch the iourney, the judgment of Alahayam now following him. For he had spoken proudly in this sort, þ he would come to Jerusalem, & make it a common burying place of þ Jews.

But the Lord almightie, the Alahayam of Yahsharala smote him with an incurable and inuisible plague: for assoone as he had spoken these words, a paine of the bowels that was remediles, came on him, & sore torments of the inner parts.
And that most iustly: for he had tormented other mens bowels with many and strange torments.

Howbeit he nothing at all ceased from his bragging, but still was filled with pride, breathing out fire in his rage against the Jews, and commanding to haste the iourney: but it came to passe that he fel down frō his chariot, caried violently, so that hauing a sore fal, al the mēbers of his body were much pained.

And thus he that a little afore thought he might command the waues of the sea (so proud was he beyond the condition of man) and weigh the high mountaines in a ballance, was now cast on the ground, and carried in an horselitter, shewing foorth to all, the manifest power of Alahayam.
So that the wormes rose up out of the body of this wicked man, & whiles he lived in sorrow and paine, his flesh fell away, and the filthinesse of his smell was noysome to all his army.
And the man that thought a little afore he could reach to the starres of heaven, no man could endure to carry for his intollerable stinke.
Here therefore being plagued, he began to leaue off his great pride, and to come to the knowledge by the scourge of Alahayam, his paine encreasing every moment.

And when he himself could not abide his own smell; he saide these wordes: It is meete to be subiect to Alahayam, and that a man that is mortall, should not proudly thinke of himself, as if he were Alahayam.
This wicked person vowed also to the Lord, (who now no more would have mercy on him) saying thus:
That the holy city (to the which he was going in haste to lay it even with the ground, & to make it a common burying place) he would set at liberty.

And as touching the Jews, whom he had iudged not worthy so much as to be buried, but to be cast out with their children to be deuoured of the foules, and wild beasts, he would make them al equals to þ citizens of Athens,

And the holy Temple, which before he had spoiled, he would garnish with goodly gifts, and restore all the holy vessels with many more, and out of his own reuenew defray the charges belonging to the sacrifices:
Yea, and that also he would become a Jew himself, and goe through all the world that was inhabited, and declare the power of Alahayam.

But for all this his paines would not cease: for the just judgment of Alahayam was come upō him: therfore despairing of his health, he wrote to the Jews the letter vnderwritten, containing the forme of a supplicatiō, after this maner.
Antiochus king and gouernour, to the good Jews his Citizens, wisheth much ioy, health, and prosperity.
If you, and your children fare well, and your affaires be to your contentment, I give very great thankes to Alahayam, hauing my hope in heaven.

As for mee I was weake, or else I would have remembred kindly your honour, and good will. Returning out of Persia, and being taken with a grieuous disease, I thought it necessary to care for the common safety of all:
Not distrusting mine health, but hauing great hope to escape this sicknes
But considering that even my father, at what time he led an armie into the hie countries, appointed a successor,
To the end, that if any thing fell out contrary to expectation, or if any tidings were brought that were grieuous, they of the land knowing to whom the state was left, might not be troubled.

Again considering, how that the princes that are borderers, and neighbors to my kingdome, waite for opportunities, and expect what shall be the euent, I have appointed my son Antiochus king, whom I often cōmitted, and cōmended to many of you, when I went up into the high prouinces, to whom I have written as followeth.
Therefore I pray, and request you to remember the benefits that I have done to you generally, and in speciall, and that every man will be still faithfull to me, and my son.
For I am perswaded that he understanding my mind, will fauourably & graciously yeeld to your desires.
Thus the murtherer, and blasphemer hauing suffered most grieuously, as he entreated other men, so died he a miserable death in a strange country in the mountaines.
And Philip that was brought up with him, caried away his body, who also fearing the son of Antiochus, went into Egypt to Ptolomeus Philometor.
Now Maccabeus, and his company, the Lord guiding them, recouered the Temple, and the city.
But the altars, which the heathen had built in the open street, & also the Chappels they pulled down.
And hauing cleansed the Temple, they made another Altar, and striking stones, they tooke fire out of them, and offered a sacrifice after two yeeres, & set forth incense, & lights, and Shewbread.

When that was done, they fell flat down, and besought the Lord that they might come no more into such troubles: but if they sinned any more against him, that he himself would chasten them with mercie, and that they might not be deliuered to the blasphemous, and barbarous nations.
Now on the same day that the strangers prophaned the Temple, on the very same day it was cleansed again, even the five and twentieth day of the same moneth, which is Casleu.

And they kept eight days with gladnes as in the feast of the Tabernacles, remembring that not long afore they had helde the feast of the Tabernacles, when as they wandered in the mountaines, and dennes, like beasts.
Therefore they bare branches, and faire boughes and palmes also, and sang Psalmes to him, that had given them good successe in clensing his place.
They ordeined also by a common statute, and decree, That every yeere those days should be kept of the whole nation of the Jews.
And this was the ende of Antiochus called Epiphanes.
Now will we declare the acts of Antiochus Eupator, who was the son of this wicked man, gathering briefly the calamities of the warres.
So when he was come to þ crowne, he set one Lysias over the affaires of his Realme, and chiefe gouernour of Coelosyria and Phenice.
For Ptolomeus that was called Macron, chosing rather to do justice to the Jews, for the wrong that had been done to them, endeuoured to continue peace with them.

Whereupon being accused of friends, before Eupator, & called traitor at every word, because he had left Cyprus that Philometor had cōmitted to him, & departed to Antiochus Epiphanes; and seeing that he was in no honorable place, he was so discouraged, that he poysoned himself and died.
But when Gorgias was gouernour of the holds, he hired souldiers, and nourished warre continually with the Jews:

And therewithall the Idumeans hauing gotten into their handes the most commodious holdes, kept the Jews occupied, and receiuing those that were banished from Jerusalem, they went about to nourish warre.
Then they that were wich Maccabeus made supplication, & besought Alahayam, that he would be their helper, and so they ranne with violence on the strong holds of the Idumeans,
And assaulting them strongly, they wanne the holds, and kept off all that fought on the wall, and slew all that fell into their hands, and killed no fewer then twenty thousand.
And because certain (who were no lesse then nine thousand) were fled together into two very strong castles, hauing all maner of things conuenient to sustaine the siege,
Maccabeus left Simon, & Joseph, and Zaccheus also, and them that were with him, who were enow to besiege them, and departed himself to those places, which more needed his helpe.

Now they that were with Simon, being led with couetousnes, were perswaded for money (through certain of those that were in the castle) and tooke seuentie thousand drachmes, and let some of them escape.

But when it was told Maccabeus what was done, he called the gouernours of the people together, and accused those men, that they had sold their brothers for money, & let their enemies free to fight against them.
So he slew those that were found traitors, and immediatly tooke the two castles.
And hauing good successe with his weapons in all things he tooke in hand, he slew in the two holdes, more then twenty thousand.
Now Timotheus whom the Jews had overcome before, when he had gathered a great multitude of forraine forces, and horses out of Asia not a few, came as though he would take Iewrie by force of armes.
But when he drew neere, they that were with Maccabeus, turned themselues to pray to Alahayam, and sprinckled earth on their heads, and girded their loynes with sackcloth,
And fell down at the foot of the Altar, and besought him to be mercifull to them, and to be an enemie to their enemies, and an aduersarie to their aduersaries, as the Law declareth.
So after the prayer, they tooke their weapons, & went on further from the city: and when they drew neere to their enemies, they kept by themselues.

Now the Sunne being newly risen, they ioyned both together; the one part hauing, together with their vertue, their refuge also to the Lord, for a pledge of their successe and victorie: the other side making their rage leader of their battell.
But when the battaile waxed strong, there appeared to the enemies from heaven, five comely men on horses, with bridles of golde, and two of them ledde the Jews,

And tooke Maccabeus betwixt them, and couered him on every side with their weapons, and kept him safe, but shot arrowes & lightenings against the enemies: so that being confounded with blindnesse, and full of trouble, they were killed.
And there were slaine twenty thousand and five hundred, and six hundred horsemen.
As for Timotheus himself, he fled into a very strong holde, called Gazara, where Chereas was gouernour.
But they that were with Maccabeus, laid siege against the fortresse couragiously four days.
And they þ were within, trusting to the strength of the place, blasphemed exceedingly, & vttered wicked words.

Neuerthelesse, on the fifth day early, twenty yong men of Maccabeus company, inflamed with anger because of the blasphemies, assaulted the wall manly, and with a fierce courage killed all that they met withall.

Others likewise ascending after them, whiles they were busied with them that were within, burnt the towres, and kindling fires, burnt the blasphemers aliue, and others broke open the gates, and hauing received in the rest of the army, tooke the city,
And killed Timotheus that was hidde in a certain pit, and Chereas his brother, with Apollophanes.
When this was done, they praised the Lord with Psalmes and thankesgiuing, who had done so great things for Yahsharala, and given them the victory.
Not long after this, Lysias the kings protectour & cousin, who also managed the affaires, tooke sore displeasure for the things that were done.
And when he had gathered about fourescore thousand, with all the horsemen, he came against the Jews, thinking to make the city an habitation of the Gentiles,
And to make a gaine of the Temple, as of the other Chappels of the heathen, and to set the high Priesthood to sale every yeere:
Not at all considering the power of Alahayam, but puffed up with his ten thousand footmen, and his thousand horsemen, and his fourescore Elephants.
So he came to Iudea, & drew neere to Bethsura, which was a strong town, but distant from Jerusalem about five furlongs, and he laid sore siege to it.
Now when they that were with Maccabeus heard that he besieged the holdes, they and all the people with lamentation and teares besought the Lord, that he would send a good Angel to deliuer Yahsharala.
Then Maccabeus himself first of all tooke weapons, exhorting the other, that they would ieopard themselues together with him, to helpe their brothers: so they went forth together with a willing mind.
And as they were at Jerusalem, there appeared before them on horsebacke, one in white clothing, shaking his armour of gold.
Then they praised the mercifull Alahayam altogether, and tooke heart, insomuch that they were ready not only to fight with men, but with most cruell beasts, & to pierce through wals of yron.
Thus they marched forward in their armour, hauing an helper from heaven: for the Lord was mercifull to them.
And giving a charge upō their enemies like lions, they slew eleuen thousand footmen, & sixteene hundred horsemen, and put all the other to flight.
Many of them also being wounded, escaped naked, and Lysias himself fled away shamefully, and so escaped.
Who as he was a man of understanding, casting with himself what losse he had had, and considering that the Hebrewes could not be overcome, because the Almighty Alahayam helped them, he sent to them,
And perswaded them to agree to all reasonable conditions, & that he would perswade the king, that he must needs be a friend to them.
Then Maccabeus consented to all that Lysias desired, being carefull of the common good; and whatsoeuer Maccabeus wrote to Lysias concerning the Jews, the king granted it.
For there were letters written to the Jews from Lysias, to this effect: Lysias to the people of the Jews, sendeth greeting.
Iohn and Absalon, who were sent from you, deliuered me the petition subscribed, and made request for the performance of the contents of it.
Therefore what things soeuer were meet to be reported to the king, I have declared them, and he has granted as much as might be.
If then you wil keepe your selues loyall to the state, hereafter also will I endeuour to be a meanes of your good.
But of the particulars I have given order, both to these, & the other that came from me, to commune with you.
Fare you wel. The hundred & eight and fortie yeere, the four and twenty day of the moneth Dioscorinthius.
Now the kings letter conteined these words, King Antiochus to his brother Lysias sendeth greeting.
Since our father is translated to þ gods, our will is, that they that are in our realme live quietly, that every one may attend on his own affaires.

We understand also that the Jews would not consent to our father for to be brought to the custome of the Gentiles, but had rather keepe their own manner of living: for the which cause they require of us that we should suffer thē to live after their own lawes.
Therefore our mind is, that this nation shall be in rest, and we have determined to restore them their Temple, that they may live according to the customes of their forefathers.
You will do well therefore to send to them, and grant them peace, that whē they are certified of our mind, they may be of good comfort, & ever goe cheerefully about their own affaires.
And the letter of þ king to the nation of the Jews was after this maner: king Antiochus sendeth greeting to the counsel, & the rest of the Jews
If you fare well, we have our desire, we are also in good health.
Menelaus declared to us, that your desire was to returne home, and to follow your own businesse.
Therefore they that will depart shall have safe conduct, till the thirtieth day of Xanthicus with securitie.
And the Jews shall use their own kind of meats, and lawes, as before, and none of them any maner of ways shall be molested for things ignorantly done.
I have sent also Menelaus, that he may comfort you.
Fare you wel. In the hundred, forty and eight yeere, and the fifteenth day of the moneth Xanthicus.
The Romanes also sent to them a letter containing these wordes: Quintus Memmius, & Titus Manlius embassadours of þ Romanes, send greeting to the people of the Jews.
Whatsoeuer Lysias the kings cousin has granted, with it we also are well pleased.
But touching such things as he iudged to be referred to the king: after you have aduised therof, send one forthwith, that we may declare as it is conuenient for you: for we are now going to Antioch.
Therefore send some with speed, that we may know what is your mind.
Farewell, this hundred and eight and fortie yeere, the fifteenth day of the moneth Xanthicus.
When these Couenants were made, Lysias went to the king, and the Jews were about their husbandrie.

But of the gouernours of seueral places, Timotheus, and Apollonius the son of Genneus, also Hieronymus, and Demophon, and besides them Nicanor þ gouernor of Cyprus would not suffer them to be quiet, and live in peace.

The men of Ioppe also did such an ungodly deed: they prayed the Jews that dwelt among them, to goe with their wiues, and children into the boats which they had prepared, as though they had meant them no hurt.

Who accepted of it according to the common decree of the city, as being desirous to live in peace, and suspecting nothing: but when they were gone forth into the deepe, they drowned no lesse then two hundred of them.
When Judas heard of this crueltie done to his country men, he commanded those that were with him
And calling on Alahayam the righteous judge, he came against those murtherers of his brothers, & burnt the haven by night, and set the boats on fire, and those that fled thither, he slew.
And when the towne was shut up, he went backward, as if he would returne to root out all them of the city of Ioppe.
But when he heard that þ Iamnites were minded to do in like maner to the Jews þ dwelt among them,
He came on the Iamnites also by night, and set fire on the haven, & the nauy, so that the light of the fire was seene at Jerusalem, two hundred and fortie furlongs off.
Now when they were gone from thence nine furlongs in their iourney toward Timotheus, no fewer then five thousand men on foote, & five hundred horse men of the Arabians, set on him.

Whereupon there was a very sore battell; but Judas side by the helpe of Alahayam got the victory, so that the Nomades of Arabia being overcome, besought Judas for peace, promising both to give him cattell, and to pleasure him otherwise.
Then Judas thinking indeede that they would be profitable in many things, granted them peace, wherupon they shooke hands, and so they departed to their tents.
He went also about to make a bridge to a certain strong city, which was fenced about with walles, and inhabited by people of diuers countries, and the name of it was Caspis.

But they that were within it put such trust in the strength of the walles, and prouision of victuals, that they behaued themselues rudely towards them that were with Judas, railing, and blaspheming, and vttering such words, as were not to be spoken.

Therefore Judas with his company, calling on the great Lord of the world (who without any rammes, or engines of warre did cast down Iericho in the time of Iosua) gave a fierce assault against the walles,
And tooke the city by the will of Alahayam, and made vnspeakable slaughters, insomuch that a lake two furlongs broad, neere adioining thereunto, being filled ful, was seen running with blood.
Then departed they from thence seven hundred and fifty furlongs, and came to Characa to the Jews that are called Tubieni.
But as for Timotheus they found him not in the places, for before he had dispatched any thing, he departed from thence, hauing left a very strong garrison in a certain hold:
Howbeit, Dositheus, and Sosipater, who were of Maccabeus captaines, went forth, and slew those that Timotheus had left in the fortresse, above tenne thousand men.

And Maccabeus ranged his armie by bands, & set them over the bands, and went against Timotheus, who had about him & hundred and twenty thousand men of foote, and two thousand, and five hundred horsemen.

Nowe when Timotheus had knowledge of Judas comming, he sent the women and children, and the other baggage to a fortresse called Carnion (for the towne was hard to besiege and vneasie to come to, by reason of the straitnesse of all the places.)

But when Judas his first band came in sight, the enemies (being smitten with fear, and terrour through the appearing of him that seeth all things) fled amaine, one running this way, another that way, so as that they were often hurt of their own men, and wounded with þ points of their own swords
Judas also was very earnest in pursuing them, killing those wicked wretches, of whom he slew about thirtie thousand men.

Moreouer, Timotheus himself fell into the hands of Dositheus, & Sosipater, whom he besought with much craft to let him goe with his life, because he had many of the Jews parents, and the brothers of some of them, who, if they put him to death, should not be regarded.
So when he had assured them with many words, that he would restore them without hurt according to the agreement, they let him goe for the sauing of their brothers.
Then Maccabeus marched forth to Carnion, & to the Temple of Atargatis, and there he slew five and twenty thousand persons.

And after he had put to flight, and destroyed them, Judas remooued the hoste towards Ephron, a strong city, wherin Lysias abode, and a great multitude of diuers nations, and the strong yong men kept the wals, and defended them mightily: wherin also was great prouision of engines, and darts.

But when Judas and his company had called on Almighty Alahayam (who with his power breaketh the strength of his enemies) they wanne the city, and slew twenty and five thousand of them that were within.
From thence they departed to Scythopolis, which lieth six hundreth furlongs from Jerusalem.
But when the Jews that dwelt there had testified that the Scythopolitans dealt louingly with them, and entreated them kindely in the time of their aduersitie:
They gave them thankes, desiring them to be friendly stil to them, and so they came to Jerusalem, the feast of the weekes approching.
And after the feast called Pentecost, they went foorth against Gorgias the gouernour of Idumea,
Who came out three thousand men of foot, & four hundred horsemen.
And it happened that in their fighting together, a few of the Jews were slaine.

At which time Dositheus one of Bacenors company, who was on horsbacke, and a strong man, was still on Gorgias, and taking hold of his coate, drew him by force, and when he would have taken that cursed man aliue, a horseman of Thracia comming on him, smote off his shoulder, so that Gorgias fled to Marisa.
Now when they that were with Gorgias had fought long & were wearie, Judas called on the Lord that he would show himself to be their helper, and leader of the battell.
And with that he beganne in his own language, & sung Psalmes with a lowd voyce, & rushing vnawares on Gorgias men, he put them to flight.
So Judas gathered his host, and came into the city of Odollam. And when the seventh day came, they purified themselues (as the custome was) and kept the Sabbath in the same place.
And on the day following as the use had been, Judas and his company came to take up the bodies of them that were slaine, and to bury them with their kinsmen, in their fathers graues.

Now under the coats of every one that was slaine, they found things consecrated to the idoles of the Iamnites, which is forbidden the Jews by the Law. Then every man saw that this was þ cause therefore they were slaine.
All men therefore praising the Lord the righteous Judge, who had opened the things that were hid,

Betooke themselues to praier, and besought him that the sin committed, might wholy be put out of remembrance. Besides, that noble Judas exhorted the people to keep themselues from sin, forsomuch as they saw before their eyes the things that came to passe, for the sin of those þ were slaine.

And when he had made a gathering throughout the company, to the sum of two thousand drachmes of siluer, he sent it to Jerusalem to offer a sin offering, doing in it very well, and honestly, in that he was mindfull of the resurrection.
(For if he had not hoped that they that were slaine should have risen again, it had bin superfluous and vaine, to pray for the dead.)

And also in that he perceiued that there was great favor layed up for those that died godly. (It was an holy, and good thought) wherupon he made a reconciliation for the dead, that they might be deliuered from sin.
In the hundreth forty and ninth yere it was told Judas that Antiochus Eupator was cōming with a great power into Iudea;

And with him Lysias his protector, and ruler of his affaires, hauing either of them a Grecian power of footemen, an hundred and ten thousand, and horsmen five thousand, & three hundred, and Elephants two & twenty, and three hundred charets armed hooks.
Menelaus also ioyned himself with them, and with great dissimulation encouraged Antiochus, not for the safegard of the country, but because he thought to have bin made gouernour.

But the King of kings mooued Antiochus mind against this wicked wretch, and Lysias enformed the king, that this man was the cause of all mischiefe, so that the king commanded to bring him to Berea, and to put him to death, as the maner is in that place.
Now there was in that place a towre of fifty cubites high full of ashes, and it had a round instrumēt which on every side hanged down into the ashes.
And whoever was condemned of sacriledge, or had committed any other grieuous crime, there did all men thrust him to death.
Such a death it happened that wicked man to die, not hauing so much as buriall in the earth, & that most iustly.
For inasmuch as he had committed many sins about the altar whose fire and ashes were holy, he received his death in ashes.
Now þ king came with a barbarous & hautie mind, to do far worse to þ Jews then had been done in his fathers time.

Which things when Judas perceiued, he commanded the multitude to call on the Lord night & day, that if ever at any other time, he would now also helpe them, being at the point to be put from their Law, from their country, and from the holy Temple:
And that he would not suffer the people, that had even now been but a little refreshed, to be in subiection to the blasphemous nations.

So when they had all done this together, and besought the mercifull Lord with weeping, and fasting, and lying flat on the ground three daies long, Judas hauing exhorted them, commanded they should be in a readinesse.
And Judas being apart with the Elders, determined before the kings host should enter into Iudea and get the city, to goe foorth and try the matter by the helpe of the Lord.

So when he had committed to the Creator of the world, & exhorted his souldiers to fight manfully, even to death, for the Lawes, the Temple, the city, the country, and the common-wealth, he camped by Modin.

And hauing given the watchword to them that were about him, Uictory is of Alahayam; with the most valiant and choice yong men, he went in into the kings tent by night, & slewe in the campe about four thousand men, and the chiefest of the Elephants, with all that were on him.
And at last they filled the campe with fear and tumult, and departed with good successe.
This was done in the breake of the day, because the protection of the Lord did helpe him.
Now when the king had taken a taste of the manlinesse of the Jews, he went about to take the holds by policie,
And marched towards Bethsura, which was a strōghold of þ Iews, but he was put to flight, failed, & lost of his men.
For Judas had conueyed to them þ were in it, such things as were necessary.
But Rhodocus who was in þ Jews hoste, disclosed the secrets to the enemies, therefore he was sought out, & when they had gotten him, they put him in prison.
The king treated with them in Bethsura the second time, gave his hand, tooke theirs, departed, fought with Judas, was overcome:

Heard that Philip who was left over the affaires in Antioch was desperately bent, confounded, intreated the Jews, submitted himself, and sware to all equal conditions, agreed with them, and offred sacrifice, honoured the Temple, and dealt kindly with the place,
And accepted well of Maccabeus, made him principall gouernor from Ptolemais to the Gerrhenians,
Came to Ptolemais, the people there were grieued for the couenants: for they stormed because they would make their couenants voide.

Lysias went up to the judgment seat, said as much as could be in defence of the cause, perswaded, pacified, made them well affected, returned to Antioch. Thus it went touching the kings comming and departing.
After three yeres was Judas enformed that Demetrius the son of Seleucus hauing entred by the haven of Tripolis with a great power and nauie,
Had taken the country, and killed Antiochus, and Lysias his protectour.

Now one Alcimus who had been hie Priest, and had defiled himself wilfully in the times of their mingling (with the Gentiles) seeing that by no meanes he could saue himself, nor have any more accesse to the holy Altar,

Came to king Demetrius in the hundreth and one and fiftieth yeere, presenting to him a crowne of golde, and a palme, and also of the boughes which were used solemnly in the Temple: and so that day he helde his peace.
Howbeit hauing gotten opportunity to further his foolish enterprise, being called into counsel by Demetrius, & asked how the Jews stood affected, and what they intēded, he answered therunto;
Those of the Jews that be called Asideans (whose captaine is Judas Maccabeus) nourish warre, and are seditious; and will not let the realme be in peace.
Therfore I being depriued of mine ancestors honor (I meane the hie Priesthood) am now come hither.

First verily for the vnfained care I have of things pertaining to the king, and secondly, even for that I intend the good of mine own country men: for all our nation is in no small misery, through the vnaduised dealing of them aforesaid.
Therefore, O king, seeing you know all these things, be carefull for the country, and our nation, which is pressed on every side, according to the clemency that you readily shewest to all.
For as long as Judas liueth, it is not possible that the state should be quiet.
This was no sooner spoken of him, but others of the kings friends being malitiously set against Judas, did more incense Demetrius.
And foorthwith calling Nicanor, who had been master of the Elephants, and making him gouernour over Iudea, he sent him forth,
Cōmanding him to slay Judas, & to scatter them that were him, & to make Alcimus high priest of the great Temple.
Then the heathen that had fled out of Iudea from Judas, came to Nicanor by flocks, thinking the harme and calamities of the Jews, to be their well-fare.

Now when the Jews heard of Nicanors comming, and that the heathen were up against them, they cast earth on their heads, and made supplication to him that had stablished his people for ever, and who alwayes helpeth his portion with manifestation of his presence.
So at the commandement of the captaine, they remooued straightwayes from thence, and came neere to them, at the towne of Deffaro.
Now Simon, Judas brother, had ioyned battell with Nicanor, but was somewhat discomfited, through the suddaine silence of his enemies.
Neuerthelesse Nicanor hearing of the manlinesse of them that were with Judas, and the courageousnes that they had to fight for their country, durst not try the matter by the sword.
Therefore he sent Posidonius, and Theodotus, & Mattathias to make peace.
